sections.title: Student flat enquiry
sections.context: A phone call between a new postgraduate student and a housing officer at a university accommodation office.

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: Good morning, Riverside Student Housing. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: Hello. I'm starting a master's course in September, and I'm looking for a flat close to the campus, because I'll be studying in the library late most evenings. My name is Linh Tran. That's T-R-A-N.

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: Thanks, Linh. Let me note that down. What's the most you can pay each month?

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: I'd like to keep it at six hundred and fifty pounds a month at most. It would also be good if the bills were included.

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: We have a few options in that range. Most of our flats include heating and internet in the rent, so there are no surprise bills at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: That sounds good. When can I move in?

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: All our flats are free from the first of September. If you arrive earlier, we can arrange that, but you'd pay for the extra days.

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: The first of September is fine. I don't have any furniture yet, so I'd like a flat that comes furnished.

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: All three of the flats I have in mind are furnished, with a desk, a bed and a wardrobe. Let me tell you about them. Oak House is two minutes from the bus stop, which is useful if you don't have a car.

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: Mill Court is next to a supermarket, so you can buy groceries on the way home. And Garden Lodge is right beside the riverside park, which is lovely in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: Oak House sounds convenient. Could I see it?

transcript.speaker: Officer
transcript.text: Of course. I've booked you a viewing on Thursday morning at ten. We'll meet at the main reception, so please bring a copy of your acceptance letter from the university.

transcript.speaker: Linh
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll be there. Thank you for your help.

sections.title: Walking tour of the Old Town
sections.context: A tour guide briefs a group of visitors before a morning walking tour of a historic town in Central Vietnam.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hoi An Ancient Town walking tour. My name is Duc, and I'll be your guide for the next two hours. Please gather around me. We'll meet outside the old post office on Tran Phu Street.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We're starting early this morning to avoid the afternoon heat, so let's keep moving.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A few practical points before we begin. The tour price includes bottled water and entrance tickets to several of the old houses. Please bring a sun hat, because there is very little shade in the open squares, and wear comfortable shoes, since we'll be walking on uneven streets.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Our first stop is the Japanese Covered Bridge. It was built several centuries ago, and it's one of the town's most recognisable landmarks. Please don't rush across it. The best photos are taken from the riverbank anyway.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: After that, we'll visit a lantern workshop. Many families here still make handmade lanterns, using bamboo and silk. You'll have about twenty minutes to try making one yourself.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Finally, we'll walk along the old tailors' street. Many of the tailors can make a shirt in one day if you order in the morning, so if you're interested, you can ask them at the end.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: One more thing. The night market opens after sunset, so I suggest you come back after the tour ends. The lanterns there look lovely in the evening. Thank you, and let's begin!

sections.title: Planning a cycling project
sections.context: A tutor meets a student to review the plan for a group research presentation on urban cycling. The student is presenting the plan for himself and his partner.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Come in, Ben. Let's look at your cycling project. Where have you got to?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Mia and I have decided to compare bike lanes in Amsterdam and Hanoi. We've already got figures on how many people cycle to work in each city.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The trouble is that the accident figures we found only cover 2019, so they might be out of date.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's a real weakness. Check whether the city councils have published newer figures. Now, what are your options for the presentation itself?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: We could show a short video of the bike lanes, run a live survey of the audience, include a map of cycle routes, add a cost comparison, or arrange interviews with city planners.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: With only ten minutes, you can't do everything. What have you decided?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The video would take up too much time, and interviews are hard to arrange in just a few weeks. So we think a route map and a cost comparison are the best choices.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Agreed. What about the survey idea?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: We thought about asking the audience to vote on which city is safer, but it's probably not worth it.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: I'd avoid it. A survey of thirty people won't be representative, so it's risky to draw conclusions from it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Understood. We'll drop it.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. What are you doing next week?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: I'll contact the city council to ask for the latest figures. If I can get them by Wednesday, I can update the charts.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Excellent. Can you and Mia write the draft introduction? The draft is due on Friday, and I'll read it over the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Of course. We'll send it to you on Friday morning.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Let's meet again in room fourteen next Monday to go through the draft.

sections.title: Coral reef restoration
sections.context: A university lecture on marine biology about how damaged coral reefs are restored.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at coral reef restoration. To begin, it's worth knowing how little of the ocean floor is covered by reefs. Coral reefs cover only about one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That's why losing them is such a serious problem.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The biggest threat today is rising sea temperatures. When the water gets too warm, corals lose the algae that give them their colour and their food, and many of them begin to die. Other pressures, such as pollution and overfishing, make recovery even harder.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Restoration projects usually follow two main methods. The first is coral nurseries. Scientists grow small coral fragments in nurseries, often on land or in shallow water, and then transplant them to damaged reefs. The second method is to attach fragments to artificial structures, often made of concrete, which are placed on the seabed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Early results are encouraging but not perfect. Roughly sixty percent of transplanted fragments survive their first year, which is better than many people expected. However, the survival rate depends heavily on the site and on the water conditions.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One practical rule is that divers should never touch the corals while they work. Even a light touch can damage the tissue, so the teams use special markers to show where each fragment has been placed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There is also good news about wildlife. In restored areas, fish populations often recover within two years, which tells us the wider ecosystem is responding.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Of course, all of this is expensive. A typical large project can cost about two hundred thousand dollars, and most of that money comes from government grants rather than private companies.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For next semester, the research team plans to use drone surveys to track changes across much larger areas. The results will be published in the spring, so I'd recommend keeping an eye on the journal.
